title: How a JPEG deletes 90% of your photo (and you can't tell)
description:
A JPEG deletes what your eyes are bad at seeing. First it splits brightness from color and keeps color at half width and half height: one color sample per 4 pixels, half the data gone. Then it cuts the picture into 8x8 blocks and rewrites each one as a mix of 64 patterns, from flat to fine stripes, and rounds the fine stripes hard: in a typical block more than 40 of the 64 become zero, and one short code says "the rest is zero". A 36 MB photo ends up around 3.6 MB, the 10:1 that JPEG typically achieves.

Numbers checked in code (verify.py): four real photos re-encoded at quality 90 came out 7x to 26x smaller (median 14x), with 44 to 58 of every 64 coefficients rounded to zero. Source: Wikipedia, JPEG.

facts_checked: JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression; converts RGB to Y'CbCr; chroma halved horizontally and vertically (4:2:0); 8x8 blocks; DCT = linear combination of 64 patterns; quantization rounds many high-frequency components to zero; EOB code for the rest of the block; eye less sensitive to fine color detail (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JPEG)
12 MP x 3 bytes = 36 million bytes; 4:2:0 = 1.5 of 3 bytes per pixel, half (verify.py)
DCT before rounding is exactly reversible (verify.py)
4 Wikimedia Commons photos at quality 90: 7.0x, 14.0x, 15.1x, 25.7x smaller; at the quality-75 table, 44.4 to 57.9 of 64 coefficients round to zero on average (verify.py)
On-screen block: a real 8x8 brightness block from the cat-on-snow photo, DCT coefficients before rounding and after the quality-75 table: 12 nonzero, 52 of 64 zero

beats.say: JPEG deletes about 90% of your photo. You can't tell.
It doesn't shrink the picture, and it doesn't drop pixels. It deletes exactly what your eyes are bad at.
Your 12 megapixel photo is 36 million bytes: red, green and blue for every pixel.
So first, split brightness from color. Your eyes see sharp detail in brightness, but barely in color.
Keep the color at half width and half height. One color sample for every 4 pixels. Half your file, gone.
Next, cut the picture into 8 by 8 blocks, and rewrite each one as a mix of 64 patterns, from flat to fine stripes.
Nothing's lost yet. The next step is the ruthless one.
Round off the fine stripes hard. Your eyes barely see them. In a typical block, over 40 of the 64 become zero.
Then one short code says: the rest of this block is zero.
36 megabytes becomes about 3.6. A tenth. And it looks the same.
Subscribe if you thought it just made the picture smaller.
